translations.text: And after the conquests of Alexander, emperor of the Macedonians, son of Philip, who set out from the land of Kittim when he defeated Darius, king of the Persians and Parthians, and who then reigned in his place over the land of the Greeks and Romans.
He gathered an army for great warfare, struck down fortresses, and killed many kings with the edge of his sword.
He took troops from many pagan nations, and all the lands trembled before him.
He assembled a great army and advanced across the land against all ruling powers.
And he made all the lands pay tribute.
After this he took to his bed, feverish with a fatal illness, and when he saw that he was dying,
he called his servants, his four foster brothers whom he had honored and who had been brought up with him from childhood, and divided his kingdom and gave it to them while he was still alive.
Alexander reigned for twelve years and died.
After him, his foster brothers established themselves separately, each in his own domain.
Each put on a crown after his death, and their sons succeeded them. For many years they multiplied lawlessness and filled the earth with their evils.

From them sprang an evil root, a shoot of bitterness: the lawless Antiochus, son of King Antiochus, who had been held as a hostage in the city of Rome. He became king in the one hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks.

In those days, lawless men arose from among the children of Israel and led many astray with deceptive and enticing words. They said, “Come, let us go and make a covenant and forge an alliance with all the pagan nations living around us, for ever since we separated and withdrew from them, many grievous troubles have come upon us.”
This proposal seemed pleasing to many.
Some of the people willingly went to appear before the king, and the king gave them authority to observe all the practices prescribed by the laws of the pagans.
They built temple courtyards in Jerusalem according to the customs of the pagans.
They established rules of uncircumcision for themselves, rebelled against the covenant of the holy Scriptures, joined the pagans, and willingly hastened to do evil.
When Antiochus’s kingdom prospered, he resolved to reign over the land of the Egyptians as well and to unite the two kingdoms.
He set out and marched against the land of the Egyptians with a great army, chariots, elephants, and many ships,
to wage war against Ptolemy, king of the Egyptians. Ptolemy was defeated by him and fled before him. In that battle many fell wounded.
Antiochus spread raids throughout the whole land. They advanced swiftly, quickly gathered the plunder, and captured all the fortresses of the land of the Egyptians.
After defeating the Egyptians, Antiochus returned in the one hundred and forty-third year.
He came against the city of Jerusalem with a great army.

He entered the sanctuary with great arrogance and took the golden altar, the lampstand for lighting, and all the furnishings of the treasury: the table for offerings, the cups, the basins, the censers, all the curtains, the crowns, and the golden ornamentation.

First he advanced against the temple, stripped it, and melted everything down. He took the silver and gold, the weapons and ornaments, and all the equipment for war. He took the hidden treasures that he found and all the precious vessels, and went to his own country.
He shed much blood and caused countless deaths, and he spoke boastfully with great arrogance.
And there was great mourning throughout Israel, in all their dwelling places.
Rulers and elders groaned; young women and young men grew weak, and the beauty of women faded.
The mouths of all the bridegrooms were filled with lamentation and weeping, and for all the brides, their [?] became bonds of mourning.
The earth shook because of its inhabitants, and the whole house of Jacob clothed itself in shame and disgrace.
Two years after those events, King Antiochus sent a chief tax collector to the cities of Judea, and he came to Jerusalem with a large army.
He began deceitfully to speak words of peace, and they believed him.
Then he attacked the city suddenly, struck them with terrible blows, and destroyed many people in Israel.
He took the city's plunder and set fire to all the wooden structures of its palaces. He tore down and destroyed the walls around the city and all the walls of its palace buildings.
They led the women and children into captivity and took all their livestock as their own possession.
They fortified the upper part of the city with strong walls and mighty towers, and it became for them a fortress within the fortified city.
They brought in a sinful people, lawless men, fortified it, filled it with weapons, equipped it, and filled it with provisions; and the entire army of Jerusalem
they gathered inside, and they became a great snare,
a hindrance to the sanctuary and a constant evil adversary to the house of Israel.
They shed innocent blood around the sanctuary and defiled the holy places.
After that, the inhabitants of Jerusalem fled because of them. It became a dwelling place for foreigners and became a stranger to its own offspring, for its children abandoned it.
Its sanctuary was devastated and became a wilderness. Its annual festivals turned into mourning, and its Sabbaths into shame and reproach. Its honor was disgraced.
Its glory was filled with dishonor, and its exalted position was brought down into mourning.
Decrees were sent throughout all the lands, ordering all the inhabitants of the earth to abandon their own laws and live under his one law.
All the nations accepted the king's command.
Many of the Israelites also turned to lawless worship, sacrificed to their idols, and profaned their Sabbaths.
The king sent messengers carrying decrees to Jerusalem and the cities of Judea, to make them adopt foreign laws,
to put an end to burnt offerings, offerings, and sacrifices in the sanctuary,
to profane the Sabbaths and annual festivals,
to defile the sanctuary and the consecrated things,
to erect altars, lay out grounds for pagan temples, and sacrifice pigs and mixed-breed animals.
and to leave their sons uncircumcised and defile themselves with every impurity of lawlessness, so that they would forget the law entirely and change its ordinances.
Whoever does not obey the king’s command shall be put to death.
In accordance with everything the king had written, he appointed overseers in every place.
And he commanded the cities of Judea to offer sacrifices, city by city.
Everyone who had rebelled against the law gathered around them, and they filled the land with evil.
They hemmed Israel in at every fortified place where they had taken refuge.
In the one hundred and forty-fifth year, on the twenty-fifth day of the month, he built an image of the abomination of desolation on the altar.
Throughout Judea, around the cities, they built pagan shrines, and they burned incense at every entrance to the houses and along all the city streets.
They tore up all the books of the covenant that they found and burned them with fire.
Wherever a book of the covenant was found in someone's possession, or anyone adhered to the law, the king's decree put that person to death.
Thus the decree against the Israelites was enforced harshly, to do this to those whom they found in the cities month after month.
On the twenty-fifth day of each month, they offered sacrifices on the pagan altars above the altar.
They killed the women who had circumcised their children, in accordance with the decree.
They hung the children from their mothers' necks, in accordance with the royal decree, and treated those who had performed the circumcisions and their sons in the same way.
Many of the people of Jerusalem stood firm and strengthened their resolve not to eat anything unclean. They willingly accepted death rather than defile themselves with contaminated food,
so that the holy covenants would not be profaned. And many of them died.
And there was a very great festival of rejoicing over Israel.
In those days Mattathias, a descendant of Simeon and son of John, a priest from the descendants of Joarib, arose, came from Jerusalem, and settled in the fortified caves at Modein.
He had five sons: John, who was called Gaddi;
Simon, who was called Thassi;
Judas, who was called Maccabeus;
Eleazar, who was called Avaran; and Jonathan, who was called Apphus.
When he saw the blasphemies being committed in Judea and in Jerusalem,

he began to lament within himself and said, “Woe to me! Why was it appointed for me to see the ruin of my people and to see the ruin of the holy city of Jerusalem? For she remains handed over into the hands of her enemies,
The sanctuary was delivered into the hands of foreigners, and the temple became like a man fallen from glory.
and her glorious furnishings are like a man handed over into captivity. Her children were slaughtered in her streets, and her young men by the sword of the enemies.
What nation is there that has not inherited her dominion? Or who is there that has not plundered her possessions and seized her spoils?”
All her adornment was stripped from her; instead of freedom, she was handed over to slavery.
All the beauty of our adornment, our holiness, and our glory were destroyed and plundered, and the nations defiled all these things.
What use is this life to us at all?
At that time Mattathias and his sons put their hands to their collars, tore their robes, dressed in sackcloth, and went into mourning.
Those who were forcibly pressing for apostasy came from the king and arrived in the city of Modein to offer sacrifices there.
Many of the Israelites came with them and gathered around them, and Mattathias and his sons [?].

Then those who had come from the king began to speak and said to Mattathias, “You are an honored ruler, and you are great in this city, firmly established among these people with your sons and brothers.

Now you be the first to come forward and carry out the command expressing the king’s will, as all the nations, the men of Judea, and all who live in Jerusalem have done. You will become friends of the king, and you and your sons will be honored with gold, silver, and royal letters.”

Mattathias answered in a loud voice, saying, “Even if all the nations in the king’s household obey the king’s commands, have rebelled and departed from the laws of their respective ancestors, and have chosen the king’s command,
nevertheless, I and my sons and brothers will follow the commandments of our ancestors.
Far be it from us to abandon the laws and ordinances of God!
We will not turn to the king’s commands or abandon the worship of our ancestors. We will not turn aside to the right or the left, and we will not obey the king’s command.”
While these words were still in his mouth, a Jewish man came forward in the sight of everyone to offer sacrifices before the temple, at the altar there in Modein, according to the king’s command.

When Mattathias saw this, he was stirred to zealous anger, and his kidneys shook with trembling. Filled with indignation and anger, he rushed forward in accordance with the judgment of the law, struck the Jew, and killed him there before the altar.
He also killed there the man who, by the royal command, was compelling people to offer sacrifices. He demolished the altar and destroyed the temple.
He acted out of zeal for the law, as Phinehas had done against Zimri, the son of Edom.
He began to cry out in a loud voice, saying, “Come! Let everyone who resolves in his heart to seek vengeance out of zeal for the law, and who desires to uphold the law, follow me!”
He and his brothers set out and fled into the mountains, leaving all their possessions there in the city.
At that time many who sought justice and righteousness went down into the wilderness
to settle there with their wives, children, and livestock, because the troubles afflicting them had become severe.

The king’s officers and the troops who were in the City of David were informed that some men who had dared to disregard the king’s command had gone down into the strongholds of the wilderness, and that many had joined together and gone down with them.
They set a time, armed themselves, made preparations, mounted, arrived, and surrounded the strongholds of the wilderness. They came to battle and shut them in on the Sabbath days.
First they sent messengers, began to speak with them, and said, “At least from now on obey the king’s command, and you will live.”
They began to speak from inside, saying, “We will not come out of our strongholds. We will not defile our Sabbaths according to this command of the king, nor will we transgress our law.”
When they heard these words, they intensified the battle against them and pressed the siege of the strongholds to capture them.
They neither occupied the narrow passes nor hurled stones nor closed up the strongholds, nor did they give any answer at all to their words, because it was the Sabbath day.

But they only encouraged one another, saying, “Let us die here in our indignation, for heaven and earth are witnesses for us that you are destroying us without cause, though we are innocent. It is better for us to die than to transgress the laws and profane the Sabbaths.”
When they heard this, they intensified the battle on the Sabbath day and killed a thousand of them, besides the people and livestock they led away into captivity.
When Mattathias and his brothers heard this, they mourned deeply and were greatly distressed.

They began speaking to one another, saying, “If we all follow the example of our brothers, who did not go out to fight against the Gentiles for their lives and their laws, then before long they will destroy us even more quickly than the first ones.”

Then they gathered, made a covenant, and took counsel together, saying, “Whenever anyone comes against us to fight on the Sabbath days, let us fight boldly, so that we are not all destroyed together like our brothers who had escaped into the wilderness there.”
At that time many troops of the Hasideans gathered to them, a mighty and warlike company from the children of Israel, every man willingly fighting for the laws.
All who were fleeing their various troubles came and joined them, strengthening their forces.

They formed an army, assembled a company, and made preparations. They struck the sinners with the force of their anger and the lawless troops with their furious wrath, driving the remaining fugitives among the Gentiles.
Mattathias pursued them with his brothers and friends, overtaking and striking them, laying waste the temples and demolishing the altars.
He circumcised the uncircumcised children and grew strong throughout the territory of the Israelites.
He drove the sons of arrogance into exile, and the work prospered in their hands.
To attend to the law, to take vengeance on the Gentiles, and to abolish the king’s unlawful decree; and they did not allow the horn of arrogance to rise.

When the days drew near for Mattathias to die, he called his sons before him and said to them, “Now pride and arrogance have become firmly established, and the time of rebuke, destruction, and pride has arrived.
But now, my children, come and be zealous for the laws. Give your lives in exchange for the covenants of your fathers.
Remember the deeds of your fathers, the acts of courage they performed in their respective generations. Gain the glory of greatness and inherit an everlasting name.
Was not Abraham found faithful in the ordeal of testing, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?
Joseph kept the commandment in the time of his affliction and became lord over the land of the Egyptians.
Phinehas our father was fervently zealous for righteousness and received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.
Joshua son of Nun became judge of the children of Israel by upholding and fulfilling the Lord’s commands.
Caleb became master of his inheritance because he bore witness among the people.
David inherited the throne of an everlasting kingdom because of his gentleness, righteousness, and mercy.
Elijah was taken up into heaven because of his fervent zeal in seeking vengeance for the laws.
Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were saved by their faith from the fire in the furnace.
Daniel was delivered from the lions’ mouths because of his sincere resolve.
Consider, then, that all who have trusted in him throughout their generations will not grow weak.
Do not be afraid of the words of an ungodly man, for his glory is filth.
Today and tomorrow, and then he is found no more, for he returns to his dust, and all his plans perish.
Be strong, children, and be courageous for the laws, for through them you will be glorified.
And here is your brother Simon. I know that he is a man of counsel. Listen to him; he shall take your father’s place.”
And Judas Maccabeus shall be your commander, the leader of your forces, and shall wage war against armies.
But you must also gather to yourselves all who observe the Law. Be zealous in seeking vengeance for your people.
Repay the nations what they deserve, and attend to the commandments of the Law.
He blessed them, and his life came to an end; he departed to his ancestors.
He died in the year 148, and they laid him in the tombs of his ancestors at Modein. All Israel mourned him with great lamentation.
His son Judas, who was called Maccabeus, arose in his place.
All his brothers and all who had followed his father became his supporters and helpers. They fought for the Israelites with gladness and joy.
And glory grew great among the people. He put on armor like a mighty warrior and equipped himself for battle. He fought great battles and sheltered the whole army with his spear.
In his deeds he was like a lion, like a young lion roaring over its prey.
He hunted down the lawless and burned those who troubled his people.
The lawless trembled in fear of him, and all who supported lawlessness were thrown into confusion. Deliverance prospered in his hands.
He embittered many kings and made Jacob glad through his deeds. His memory shall be blessed forever.
He went against the towns of Judea and wiped out the ungodly from them, turning wrath away from Israel.
He gathered those who were scattered and found those who were lost.
Then Apollonius assembled a force of Gentiles and gathered many more troops from the Samaritans to come and wage war against Israel.
When Judas saw this, he went out to meet him, struck him down, and killed him. He wounded many of his troops and put the rest to flight.
He took his spoils and plunder. Judas took Apollonius's sword, and with that very sword he struck their armies throughout his life.
When Seron [?], commander of the Syrian forces, heard that Judas had assembled a force and that many faithful men were with him, going into battle,
he considered it and said, “I too will make a name for myself and gain glory in my kingdom. I will wage war against Judas and defeat those who despise the king's command.”
Once again he assembled a force, and many troops of lawless men joined him as reinforcements, coming to seek vengeance on the Israelites.
He came as far as the region of Beth-horon. Judas went out to meet him with a few men.

When they saw the army advancing against them in battle formation, those with Judas began to speak, saying, “How can we, so few, fight against such a strongly equipped army, especially when we are exhausted and weak, having gone hungry for so long today?”
Judas began to encourage them and said, “It is an easy thing for God to deliver many into the hands of a few, and to the heavenly One there is no difference between many and few.
For victory does not depend on a large army; rather, the strength for victory comes from heaven.
They come against us in arrogant pride and lawlessness, to destroy us and lead our wives and children into captivity.”
We are fighting for our lives and for our laws.
And the Lord will destroy them before our feet. Be strong and courageous; do not be afraid.

While these words were still in his mouth, he charged the army and broke the wing where King Nren [?] stood armed. He dislodged the army and put all the troops before him to flight, together with the king.

They pursued them as far as the region of the plain of Beth-horon, leaving many of their wounded lying dead on the ground. About eight hundred of their men fell, and the survivors fled into Philistia.
Fear and dread began to go before Judas and his brothers, and thereafter they were eager to raid the Gentiles who lived around them.
His name reached the king, and the Gentiles told him about the battles.
When Emperor Antiochus heard these reports, he became furious in his anger. He mustered troops from all his lands and gathered a very large army.
He opened his treasury, distributed a year's pay to the troops, and ordered them to be ready for everything.

When he saw that the treasures were exhausted and the tribute from the country had diminished because of the division and the devastation he had brought upon the land by abolishing the ancestral laws that had existed from the earliest times
He became alarmed that he might not have enough for the payments and wages that he had previously distributed so generously.
Troubled in his mind, he decided to enter the land of Persia, collect tribute from the lands there, and amass a great deal of silver.
He left Lysias there, a distinguished man of royal lineage, in charge of the royal affairs from the region of the Euphrates to the borders of Egypt,
and to bring up his son Antiochus until he returned.
He left half the troops and the elephants with him and gave him instructions about everything he wanted and had planned, and about the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem.
He organized an expedition against them to destroy them, wipe out the strength of Israel and the remnant of Jerusalem, and erase their memory from that place,
and to settle foreigners throughout all their territory and divide up all their land by measuring lines.

He himself took half the troops and departed from the city of Antioch, from his royal residence, in the one hundred and fortieth year. He crossed the great river, the Euphrates, and traveled through the upper provinces.
Lysias chose Ptolemy [?], Nicanor, and Gorgias, powerful men who were friends and advisers of the king.

With them he assembled a force of forty thousand mounted men and seven thousand trained horses, to march into the land of Judea, strike and destroy the country, and lay the land waste according to the king's command.
They departed with all their troops, arrived, and camped near Emmaus, in the level country on the plain.

The merchants of the country heard that troops had arrived to plunder the land of Judea and carry its sons and daughters into captivity. They took their silver and gold, and as many men as they could obtain to help them, and came to buy the children of the Israelites as slaves for themselves. Syrian troops and the people of the land of the foreigners joined them.

When Judas and his brothers saw that every calamity had come upon them and that all these troops had arrived and were keeping their territory under siege, they learned of the king's orders commanding that the people be destroyed and brought to ruin.
They began speaking to one another, saying, “Come, let us strengthen ourselves, raise our people from their downfall, and fight for our holy places and our people.”
The assembly gathered to prepare for battle. They stood in prayer and asked the Lord for mercy.

Jerusalem was desolate and empty, and none of its people entered or left it. The sanctuary lay trampled underfoot by foreigners, and the fortified upper part of the city had become a dwelling place for Gentiles. Jacob’s joys were taken away; trumpets and harps ceased, and all the joyful delights of the musicians fell silent.
They all came and gathered at Mizpah, opposite Jerusalem, because Mizpah had formerly been a place of prayer for the Israelites.
They proclaimed a fast, dressed in sackcloth, took [?] and ashes, put dust on their heads, and tore their collars.
They spread out the books of the law, because of which the Gentiles were oppressing them.
They brought the priestly garments, the firstborn offspring, and the tithes into their midst. They roused and brought forward those under vows whose appointed days had been completed.
Together they cried aloud to heaven, saying, “Now what shall we do with these things, or where shall we take them?
Why have your holy places been trampled underfoot, and why do your priests sit in mourning and distress?
Look, all the Gentiles have gathered to destroy us. You know what they are plotting against us.
How, then, can we withstand them unless you help us?”
They blew the trumpet, raised a shout, and cried aloud to heaven.
After this, Judas began organizing the people and appointed leaders over them: commanders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
They spoke to those who were building houses, becoming engaged to women, and planting vineyards, and instructed the fainthearted to return to their homes according to the law.
The whole army arrived and camped behind Emmaus.

Then Judas began encouraging the troops, saying, “Arm yourselves, prepare yourselves, and be strong, so that in the morning you may fight these Gentiles who have gathered against us to destroy us and our holy places.
For it is better for us to die in battle than to see the suffering of our people and our holy places.
Whatever the Lord’s will in heaven may be, let it be fulfilled.
May he remember the covenant and its promises to our fathers, and crush this army beneath our feet.
Let the Gentiles know that there is a God who saves Israel.”
They raised their eyes toward the foreigners and saw that they were advancing to attack them.
They went out ahead of the army into battle. On Judas’s side they blew the trumpet.
They gathered together, charged, engaged in combat, and put them to flight.

They killed many on the spot and drove many into flight across the plain. They fell by the edge of their swords as far as the borders of Gazara, in the territory of the Edomites, and at Azotus and Jamnia. About three thousand men fell wounded that day.
Judas returned with his troops, and as he came he reached the battlefield.
He began speaking to the troops, saying, “Do not turn your eyes toward the plunder or the stripping of the fallen bodies.
For that Gorgias still stands armed and ready against us with his forces. But stand firm, hold your position, and withstand your enemies. Then, after victory in battle, return with confidence.
While he was speaking these words to them, they saw a company appear from the mountain.
They realized that a defeat had taken place and that they had begun setting fire to the camp there. The rising smoke was a sign of what had happened.
When they saw this, they hesitated, especially when they looked at Judas's company, drawn up and ready for battle.
They took to their heels and fled to the land of the Philistines.

Judas returned to the battlefield to plunder, loot, and take spoils from the bodies of the fallen. From their camp he took gold and silver, costly garments, scarlet and blue cloth, purple cloth dyed from the sea, and great wealth.
When they returned from there, they began to give thanks and bless the Lord in heaven, saying, “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”
That day brought great deliverance to Israel.
All those among the foreigners who had escaped came and reported to Lysias everything that had happened.

When Lysias heard this, he was grieved, bowed down, and fell on his face, because his plans against the Israelites had not been accomplished as he intended, and the command the king had given him had not been carried out.
When the next year came, he raised an army, assembling men and horses: about six thousand infantry and five thousand fully armed cavalry, to come and plunder the land of Judea.
They came, arrived, and drew up for battle in the region of Beth-zur. Judas went out to meet them with eleven thousand men.

When they saw the large and powerful company, they began to pray and bless God, saying, “Lord God, you are the one who shattered the strength of the mighty attacker through your servant David and delivered the armies of the foreigners into the hands of Jonathan son of Saul.
Now shatter the strength of these forces through the hands of Israel. Let their power be extinguished, together with their horses and troops.
Cast cowardice upon them and drive away the strength of their pride. Let them be shaken to their downfall.
Bring them down and deliver them to the sword of those you love, and let those who know your name bless you with praises.”
They clashed face to face, and at that time five thousand cavalry from Lysias's company fell before them.

When Lysias saw the defeat of his company and the courageous victory of Judas's company, and how they were ready to live or die for the honor of a valiant victory, he departed, marched away, and went to the region of Antioch. There he again gathered an army, organizing and preparing it to invade the region of Judea once more.

Judas, together with his brothers, began speaking to the people and said, “Look, our enemies have been crushed beneath our feet. Come, let us go and purify the holy places, purify the temple, and celebrate its dedication.”
The whole assembly gathered and came to Mount Zion.

They saw the sanctuary devastated, the altar defiled, and the gates burned. Bushes were growing throughout the courts as in a forest or on the mountains. The basins were demolished, and the curtain supports were damaged.
They thrust their hands into their collars, tore their robes, and put earth on their heads.
They rolled on the ground, sounded trumpet signals, and cried out to heaven.
At that time Judas gave orders and assigned troops to besiege the citadel while he purified the holy places.
He chose blameless priests who obeyed the law.
He purified the sanctuary, and they removed the stones that had been defiled and set them aside in a separate place.
And they deliberated about what to do with the altar of burnt offerings, which had been defiled by the enemies.

In their deliberations there, they resolved to tear down the altar because it had been defiled by their enemies, so that it would not remain a burden on their conscience and an everlasting reproach. And they tore down the altar.
And they carried the stones away and placed them in a suitable place until a prophet should come and speak about them.
And they took unhewn stones according to the law and built the sanctuary.
And there was nothing inside the temple there, and they cleansed the courts.
And they made new sacred utensils and brought inside the lampstand for lighting, the incense altar, and the table of the temple.
And they burned incense on the altar, lit lamps, and gave light to the temple.
They placed the daily bread on the table, hung the curtains, and completed all the work of the service they were performing.
They rose early in the morning on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, in the one hundred and fortieth year.
They offered a sacrifice according to the law on the altar of burnt offerings, which they had newly made, at the appointed time.
On the very days when the Gentiles had defiled it, at that same time it was rededicated with songs of praise, with trumpet, lyre, and flute.
And all the people fell on their faces; they fell down, bowed in worship, and blessed God in heaven, who had granted them success.
And they celebrated the dedication of the altar for eight days, offered burnt offerings with joy, and offered sacrifices of deliverance and praise.
They adorned the basins and the curtain rods in front of the temple with gold crowns and gold plates, and they restored the gates and set them up.
There was exceedingly great joy among the people, and the reproach inflicted by the Gentiles was wiped away from them.

And Judas, together with his brothers and the whole assembly of the Israelites, decreed that these days of the dedication of the altar should always be observed at their appointed time, year after year in the annual cycle, for eight days beginning on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, with joy and gladness.
And at that time they built high walls and fortified towers all around Mount Zion, lest the Gentiles should come and trample them as they had done before.
And he left a force to guard it and strengthened it to besiege Beth-zur, so that it would be a stronghold for the forces on the borders of the Edomites.
When the surrounding Gentiles heard that the altar had been rebuilt and the sanctuary restored once again as it had been before, they became very angry.
They planned to come and wipe out the descendants of Jacob who lived among them, and they began to slaughter and destroy them.

And Judas continually waged war against the descendants of Esau who were in the territory of the Edomites in Akrabattene, because they had come from all around and were encamped, surrounding and besieging Israel. He struck them with many blows, reduced their numbers, and took their plunder and spoils.
And he remembered the wickedness of the descendants of Baean, who had become a snare and a stumbling block to the people, throwing them into confusion on their journeys.
They fled from him and fortified themselves in their strongholds. He came, posted guards around them, and set fire to their strongholds together with all their inhabitants.
He crossed over and advanced against the Ammonites. There he found a powerful force, many troops, and Timothy their commander.
He attacked them head-on and many times pressed the battle fiercely against them.
He struck them, drove them away, and captured the city of Jazer and its dependent towns, and returned to the territory of Judea.
All the Gentiles in Gilead gathered against the Israelites who lived in their territory, intending to destroy them. The Israelites fled into the stronghold at Dothaim.
And they sent messengers to Judas and his brothers, saying, “Look, all the Gentiles have gathered against us. They have surrounded and besieged us and are determined to wipe us out of this place.
They are ready to take the strongholds in which we have taken refuge, and Timothy is their commander.
Now, if there is anything you can do, hurry to rescue us from their hands, for many of us have fallen.”

And all the brothers who were in Tob were slaughtered, and their wives and children were led into captivity with all their goods and possessions. They all perished, throughout one district under a single chief commander of a thousand.
While the letters were still in their hands, other messengers of disaster arrived from the districts of Galilee, with their clothes torn and their foreheads bruised, and brought this bad news:
They said, “The Gentiles from Ptolemais, Tyre, Sidon, and all the districts of Galilee have gathered against us to wipe us out of there.”

When Judas and the people heard these words, they quickly gathered in council to consider what they should do for the brothers who were in distress and suffering at the hands of those waging war against them.

Judas began speaking to his brother Simon and said, “Choose strong men for yourself and go to rescue the brothers who are in distress in the districts of Galilee. My brother Jonathan and I will go to the districts of Gilead.”
He left Joseph son of Zechariah and Zacharias, the commander, there with carefully selected troops to guard the land of Judea.
He gave them orders, saying, “Lead this people, but do not engage the Gentiles in battle until we return from there.”
They divided the army into two detachments. Three thousand went with Simon to the districts of Galilee, and eight thousand went to the land of Gilead.
Simon went to the land of Galilee and fought against the Gentiles. The Gentiles were crushed before him, and he pursued them as far as the gates of Ptolemais.
On that day, three thousand fully armed men from among the Gentiles fell.

He took their spoils from the districts of Galilee and from Arbatta, together with the women and children, all their possessions, and their valuable goods. They came and brought all this to the land of Judea with rejoicing and gladness.
Judas Maccabeus and his brother Jonathan crossed to the other side of the Jordan River and traveled for three days into the wilderness.
The Nabateans met them peacefully and told them everything that had happened to the brothers in the land of Gilead.
Many of them had been carried off as captives to the cities of Bosora, Bosaluma [?], Sephor [?], Maked, and Zarnaspasia [?]. These cities are fortified and very large.

And those from the other cities in the districts of Gilead have gathered together in one place. They have agreed that tomorrow they will blockade and surround the fortresses, capture them, and wipe out and kill everyone in a single day.

When Judas heard this, he quickly formed a detachment and took the road through the wilderness. He suddenly fell upon Bosora and, suddenly, at an unexpected hour, seized the whole city. There he put every male youth to the sword, took all the spoils of the city of Bosora, and set the whole city on fire.
During the night, he advanced with his detachment toward the fortress of those under siege.

Just as morning was about to emerge from the night, they raised their eyes and saw a vast, innumerable army carrying ladders, catapults, and various siege engines. They had launched an attack on the fortress and advanced into battle.

When Judas looked and saw that the fighting had begun, the cries from the city on one side and from the troops maintaining the siege on the other—the sound of combat, the sound of battle, and the sound of the trumpet—all rose together to heaven.
He began to speak to his troops and said, “Come, be courageous and stand firm! Today your task is to fight for your brothers.”
He divided all his troops into three companies, drew them up around the enemy, and led them into battle. They sounded the trumpet, raised a cheer, cried out in prayer to God, and attacked.

Timothy and his troops were told that Maccabeus had arrived with his army to attack them. When they looked and saw him, they were alarmed, lost heart, and faltered. They abandoned their equipment and turned to flee. That day he struck them with severe blows. His men drove the fugitives before them, making them fall dead one after another, and put about eight hundred thousand fully armed men to the sword.
He himself turned toward Mizpah, fought against it, and captured it. There he killed all their male children, took all their goods and possessions as plunder, and burned the city with fire.
From there he set out and came and besieged Casphor, Maked, Bosor, and the remaining cities of Gilead.
After these events Timothy gathered an army again and came and camped opposite Raphon, on the other side of the river.
Judas sent scouts to inspect their camp. They returned and reported, “All the nations and peoples encamped around us have gathered together, and a very large force has assembled.”
“He has also hired many [?] to help them. They are encamped on the other side of the river, ready to come and attack you.” When Judas heard this, he immediately set out and advanced against them.

When Timothy saw him, he began speaking to his commanders and said, “Watch Judas and his company as they reach the riverbank. If he crosses as soon as he arrives, we will not be able to withstand him, for he will certainly defeat us.”
“But if he reaches the riverbank and draws up his battle line there, it will show that he is afraid. We will cross over, fight, and defeat him.”

While these words were still in his mouth, Judas arrived with his troops at the riverbank. There he stationed the muster clerks along the bank and commanded them not to allow anyone at all to camp beside the river, but to send every fighting man across after him.

But Judas arrived, crossed, and attacked all at once. First he broke through the company of their fighting men, then put the entire army to flight. All the nations and peoples threw down their weapons and fled to the stronghold, to the sacred precinct of the temple in Carnaim.
Judas and his men arrived, surrounded the city, and set fire to the stronghold together with the temple. Carnaim was hard pressed and could not withstand Judas.

Judas ordered all the Jews who were in the regions of Gilead to set out with their wives, children, and all their belongings, and to be brought into the land of Judea. They formed very large companies.

They came to the gate of the city of Ephron. This was a large city on the road, in a fortified location, and there was no other route by which they could turn aside to the right or the left; they had to pass through the city.

When the city's troops saw the mass of soldiers and the great number of companies, they closed the gates, blocked the entrances with stones, and would not let them pass. When Judas saw this, he sent them a peaceful message.

He said, “Allow me to pass through your territory and go on to my own country. No one will do you any harm; we will only tread your land with our feet.” But they would not agree to open the gates for him.
Then Judas ordered the trumpet to be sounded and a proclamation to be made: “Come, let each company advance into the city from wherever it stands!”
And the troops advanced from each place where they were stationed to engage in battle. They fought all day and all night until the city was delivered into their hands.

There they killed all their male children with the edge of their swords and uprooted them. They carried away the city's plunder, and they themselves passed through the city, walking over the bodies of the fallen.
They crossed the Jordan River into the level country, onto a broad plain, and camped there opposite Beth-shan.
There Judas looked after the welfare of the people and encouraged everyone. He did this throughout the entire march until he brought them into the land of Judea.

And they came and went up to Mount Zion with rejoicing and gladness. There they offered burnt offerings and sacrifices, because none of them had perished before they returned to their own place in peace.
In those days Judas and Jonathan were in the land of Gilead, and Simon their brother was in the land of the Galileans, opposite Ptolemais. When they heard of these brave deeds in battle,
Joseph son of Zechariah and Zechariah, the commander of the troops that remained,
said, “Come, let us also go and wage war against the Gentiles around us, and let us too make a name for ourselves.”
They gave the troops the signal, set out, and went toward Jamnia.
Gorgias came out of the city with the troops who were with him to do battle, and attacked them.
Joseph and Zechariah were defeated and fled under pursuit as far as the borders of Judea. That day about two thousand of their men fell, and this was a severe disaster for the people.
For they had not obeyed Judas and his brothers, but had thought, “We too will win a name for bravery like him.”
But they were not descended from those men into whose hands the deliverance of Israel had been entrusted.
And Judas himself and his brothers were honored in the eyes of the people and before all the Gentile nations, wherever their names were heard.
People gathered and blessed them.

Judas went out with his brothers to wage war against the descendants of Esau in the southern region. There he attacked the city of Hebron and its surrounding towns, tore down and destroyed all their fortifications, and burned its towers all around, wherever he found them.
Then he set out and proceeded into the land of the Philistines, reaching the region of Marisa.
That day priests fell in battle there while he still wanted to perform some feat of bravery, for he had gone out to wage war without taking counsel.

Judas turned toward Azotus in the land of the Philistines. He devastated their temples, demolished their idols, and burned their cities. He carried off their goods and possessions as plunder and returned to the land of Judea.
Emperor Antiochus was traveling through the upper provinces when he heard that there was a city in the region of Elymais, in the land of Persia, a splendid city full of gold and silver.

The temple in it possessed very great treasures, and there were large cast-gold idols in it. There were also many weapons, suits of armor, and sheaths that Alexander, emperor of the Macedonians, who first ruled over the land of the Greeks, had left there.
He came to that city and sought to take it as plunder. The citizens were informed,
and they prepared for battle and did not allow him to enter. He was struck with fear, departed, and went from the eastern regions into the land of the Babylonians.
There a messenger bearing bad news came to Emperor Antiochus from the southern regions, reporting that the troops that had gone into Judea had been defeated.

For Lysias had gone on the first campaign with many troops and had been defeated before them. They had grown strong in weapons and troops and had amassed much plunder. They had destroyed their camps and carried off their goods and possessions as plunder.
They demolished the temples and destroyed the idols that had been set up on the altar in Jerusalem. They enclosed the sanctuary with high walls as before, and likewise the city of Beth-zur.
When the king heard these things, he was astonished, amazed, stunned, and deeply troubled. He took to his bed and became ill because the purpose of his command had not been fulfilled.
He lay there for many days, for many sorrows came upon him afresh. He thought, “I am dying.”
He called all his friends and said to them, “Sleep has departed from my eyes, and my heart is [?] with my worries.
I spoke with my heart and said, ‘To what depths of distress have you come, and into what great turmoil, in which I am now trapped! For I was kind and generous, and beloved by my troops.’
Now I remember the evils I committed in Jerusalem: I took all those gold and silver vessels, and I also assembled troops against them without cause, to destroy them.
Now I know that this is why all these evils have overtaken me, and here I am perishing in sorrow in a foreign land.”
He called Philip, one of his friends, and appointed him over his entire kingdom.
He gave him his crown, robe, and ring, to bring up his son Antiochus, raise him, and make him king in his place.
King Antiochus died there in the one hundred and forty-ninth year.
Lysias was informed that the king had died. He made his son Antiochus king and gave him the name Antiochus Eupator.
Those who were shut up in the citadel oppressed Israel, continually sought to do harm around the sanctuary, and were a source of strength for the Gentiles.
The citizens decided to destroy them. And when he had gathered all the companies of troops,
they came and encamped around them, gathered together in one place, and besieged it. In the one hundred and fiftieth year, they built siegeworks, missile engines, and many siege machines.
Some came out of the enclosure and joined lawless men from among the Israelites.
They went to the king and said, “How long will you refrain from administering justice and avenging our brothers?
We agreed to serve your father and follow his commands.
For this reason, members of our people besieged it, and many became estranged from us. Those of us whom they found, they put to death, and they handed over our inheritances to be plundered.
They have raised their hands not only against us, but also throughout all their own territory.
Now they have come and surrounded us in a siege. Look, they have come and shut in the citadel of Jerusalem, keeping it under siege to capture it, and they have fortified the sanctuary and Beth-zur.
If you do not hurry quickly, they will do still greater things than these, and you will not be able to stop them.”
When the king heard this, he became very angry and ordered his friends and the commanders of the troops to be summoned.
Many mercenary troops came to him from another kingdom and from other islands.
His troops numbered one hundred thousand infantry carrying shields and spears, twenty thousand fully armed cavalry, and thirty-two elephants equipped for battle as mounts.

They came through Edom, drew up for battle, and surrounded the city of Beth-zur, waging war against it for many days. They set up mangonels and siege machines around it. But men came out of the city, burned the siege machines, and fought them bravely.
Judas broke camp and departed from the fortified citadel. He came and encamped at Beth-zechariah, directly opposite the king’s army.
Early in the morning the king took the army, led it away from there, and encamped along the road to Beth-zechariah. He spread out the troops and drew them up for battle, and they sounded the trumpet.
They equipped and prepared the elephants and gave them grape juice, mulberries, and wine to taste.

They arranged and divided themselves into separate units. Beside each elephant they stationed a thousand fully armed men, and at the head of the units they placed five thousand horsemen on equipped steeds to guard and protect the units.
Wherever the beasts stood, they too would stand, and wherever the beasts went, they too would go.
They constructed enclosed fighting platforms with engines on the elephants and seated each elephant-driver above its head.
They stationed the rest of the cavalry on the right and left wings of the army.
When the sun cast its first rays upon the bronze-covered shields of the armored, fully armed men, their gleams flashed across the mountains, and rays shot out like flashes of fire.
The battle line stretched out and spread over the mountain heights, through the valleys and depths, and across the plains.

They advanced together, arranged and equipped, all moving in unison, hearing the roar of the multitude, the clash of weapons, the thunder of the horses, and the pounding footsteps of the armed shield-bearers.

Judas arrived with his unit. They took their positions, equipped themselves, formed a battle line, and prepared. He charged forward and struck the king’s division. There, in the king’s presence, he left six hundred fully armed horsemen piled dead before the king.
There Eleazar Avaran raised his eyes to look and saw one of the beasts equipped and adorned with royal armor and displaying royal insignia. He thought that the king himself must be on it.
He charged the division, cutting men down on his right and left, and went on until he reached the elephant bearing the insignia. He raised his weapon
and went underneath it, struck it, and brought it down there.
The elephant sank down upon him and crushed him there.
When they saw the strength of the king’s forces, they fled from them.
But whichever way they went, the royal divisions met them, until they reached the region of Jerusalem. The king came, and they encamped in Judea and at Mount Zion.

He negotiated a peaceful settlement with the city of Beth-zur, and its people came out and dispersed from the city, because they had no provisions there. They had been blockaded and besieged for a long time, and that year happened to be a sabbath year throughout the land.
The king took the city of Beth-zur and ordered troops to be brought inside to guard the city.

He himself kept the holy city under siege for many days. Around it they set up mangonels, siege engines, fire-throwers, stone-throwers, machines for hurling great stones, ballistas, towers for shooting arrows, and towers for slingers.
Those inside the city, in turn, began constructing engines to counter their engines, and they engaged in battle and fought for many days.
But they could find no provisions, because that was the seventh year throughout the land, and the refugees in the country had consumed the stored provisions.
Only a few remained in the sanctuary, because the others had dispersed to their own places. The famine had become severe among them, and they scattered, each to his own place.
When Lysias heard about Philip, whom Antiochus himself had ordered to bring up his son Antiochus so that he might establish him as king,
When he returned from Persia and Parthia, all the troops joined him, and he himself wished to take charge of the affairs of the kingdom.

he came and said to the king and all the commanders of the forces, “The troops are continually in distress, the provisions have dwindled, and food is scarce. The place against which we are fighting is strongly fortified and impossible to take, and the affairs of the kingdom demand our attention.”
Now come, let us speak of reconciliation, make a treaty, and establish peace with the men of that nation.

Let us establish terms with them, allowing them each to keep their own laws as before. For it was because of their own laws, which we disrupted, that they became angry with us, entered into conflict, and did all these things.
The proposal pleased the king and his officials, and he sent messengers to speak of peace. And they accepted.
The king and his officials swore an oath to them, and then they came out of the fortresses.
The king entered Mount Zion and saw how strongly fortified the place was. He broke the oath he had sworn and ordered its surrounding walls to be torn down.
He set out quickly for the region of Antioch and found Philip in control of the city. He fought against him and took the city by force.
In the one hundred and fifty-first year, Demetrius the Seleucid departed from the city of Rome and came with a small force to a coastal city, where he became king.
When Antiochus was about to enter the royal palace of his ancestors, many troops surrounded him. They arrested Lysias and Antiochus, bound them, and brought them to Demetrius.
When they reported the matter to Demetrius, he gave an order, saying, “Do not let me see their faces at all.”
The troops took them outside, led them away, and killed them. And Demetrius sat on the royal throne.
Lawless and ungodly men from the people of Israel came before him. Alcimus was their leader, for he himself aspired to the priesthood.
They accused the people, saying, “Judas has utterly destroyed us, his brothers and your friends, and has driven us out of the land.
Now send trustworthy men to come and see the suffering of the nation and the destruction he has brought upon us, for he has devastated the king’s land and afflicted their allies.”
The emperor chose Bacchides, a friend of the king and governor of the region beyond the river, a great official faithful to his kingdom, and they sent him out.
And the lawless Alcimus was with him, and they entrusted the priesthood to him. He gave orders to take vengeance on the Israelites.
Bacchides set out and went on his way. From where he was, he sent messengers to Judas and his brothers to speak to them about peace with deceitful words.
They paid no attention to his words, for they saw that he had arrived with a large army.
Groups of scribes seeking justice began to gather before Bacchides and Alcimus.
The Hasideans were the first among the Israelites to seek peace.
For they reasoned this way: “A priest descended from Aaron has come with the army. He will not allow us to be harmed.”
He spoke peaceful words to them and swore an oath to them, saying, “I will not allow you or your friends to be harmed.”
They trusted him, but he seized sixty men from among them and killed them in a single day, according to the words that are written:
“They cast the bodies of your holy ones to the birds of heaven and poured out their blood around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.”
Dread and fear fell upon the people, for they said, “There is neither justice nor truth in them, for they have violated the agreement and the oath they swore.”
Bacchides left Jerusalem and came and encamped at Bethzeth. He sent men and seized many of the deserters and many of the people, and ordered them to be slaughtered inside the pit.
He placed the land in Alcimus’s hands and left many troops with Alcimus to assist him. Then Bacchides went to the king.
Alcimus strove to secure the high priesthood.
All those who stirred up trouble among the people gathered around him. They overpowered the land of Judah and inflicted great blows upon Israel.
When Judas saw the evils committed by Alcimus and the Israelites who were with him
He attacked Judea throughout its borders and took vengeance on the men who had willingly gone over to the Gentiles, and afterward they were prevented from returning to the land of Judea.
When Alcimus saw that Judas had grown strong once again, and realized, “I cannot withstand him,” he returned to the king to speak against him.
The king sent Nicanor, one of his distinguished commanders, who especially hated the people of Israel and was hostile toward them. He ordered him to wipe out the people from that place.
Nicanor arrived with a large army and deceitfully sent words of peace to Judas and his brothers.
“Let there be no fighting between me and you. I will come with a few men to meet you in peace.”
He came to Judas, and they greeted one another peacefully, but the troops were drawn up and ready to attack and seize Judas.
When Judas was informed that Nicanor had come to deal deceitfully with him, he became troubled, drew back, rejected him, and withdrew. He no longer wished to see him.
When Nicanor saw that his plan had been revealed to Judas, he set out to meet him in battle in the region of Capharsalama.
About five hundred men fell on Nicanor’s side, and the rest fled into the City of David.
After these events, Nicanor went up to Mount Zion. Some of the holy priests came out to meet him, to greet him peacefully and show him the burnt offerings that they offered daily for the king’s life.
But he treated them with contempt, laughed at them, and defiled them with proud and arrogant words.

He struck them and said angrily, “If you do not hand Judas and his army over to me, let things be as they are for now; but if I return safely, I will punish this temple with fire and take vengeance on you.” Then he went away in fury and great anger.
The priests went in and stood before the altar and the temple. They began to weep and said:
“You chose this temple of yours to have your holy name called upon it, so that it might be a house for the vows and petitions of your people.
Take vengeance on this man and his army, and let them fall by their own swords. Remember their blasphemies, and give them no rest.”
Nicanor left Jerusalem and camped at Beth-horon, and Assyrian troops came to meet him.
Judas himself was camped at Adasa with three thousand men. He began to pray and said:

“When those who came from the king blasphemed, your angel went out and struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand of them, destroying them there. In the same way, destroy this army today, so that those who remain may know that he spoke vainly against your sanctuary. Judge him according to his wickedness.”

The two battle lines approached one another and clashed on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar. Nicanor’s army was defeated and crushed, and he himself was the first to fall by the sword between the two battle lines.
When the army saw that Nicanor had fallen, they threw down their weapons and turned to flee.
Judas’s men pursued them for a day, from Adasa until they reached Gazara, sounding signal trumpets as they followed them.

People came out from all the surrounding towns of Judea and cut them down. Turning back toward one another, the fugitives gathered together against one another, and that day they all fell by the sword. Not one of them remained.

They came and joined in taking the spoil, the plunder, the weapons, the treasure, and the equipment of the camp. They brought Nicanor’s head, together with his right hand, which he had arrogantly dared to stretch out toward the temple, and hung it up in view of Jerusalem.
The people rejoiced greatly and made that day a great annual celebration.
They decreed that this day, the thirteenth of the month of Adar, should be celebrated as a festival every year.
The land of Judah was quiet for a few days.

Judas heard of the reputation of the Romans: that they were mighty in their strength, that they looked favorably on anyone who sought their support and became their ally, and that they had become powerful throughout the earth.
He also heard about their battles, how they had courageously struck the territories of the Galatians, overpowered them, and subjected them to tribute.

He heard about everything they had done in the territories of the Spaniards, how they had seized from them the mines from which gold and silver are extracted. Through their planning and patience they had taken possession of all those places, although the region was very far from them.

He also heard about the kings who had come against them from the ends of the earth, whom they had struck down. They inflicted crushing defeats on them and destroyed them, and subjected the survivors to the payment of tribute every year.
They destroyed Philip and the king of the [?], who had risen against them, in battle and defeated them.
Antiochus the Great, king of Asia, had come against them in a great war, bringing with him one hundred and twenty elephants, chariots, and very many horses, but he was defeated by them.
They captured him alive and kept him in one place to pay tribute.
They also required the kings who succeeded him to give hostages and pledges. They took the lands of India, Parthia, and Lydia, the choicest of their provinces, and handed them over to King Eumenes.
He also heard that the Greeks had planned to come and destroy them, and when word of this reached them,

they sent one of their generals, who came and struck them down and destroyed them in a great war. They put many of them to the sword, carried their wives and children into captivity, and plundered their goods and possessions. They held the land in subjection, demolished its fortresses, and subjected the country to tribute and servitude, which continue to this day.
They also destroyed the other kingdoms and islands that rebelled and subjected them to servitude.

But they maintained steadfast friendship with their friends and those who relied on their support. They became powerful over all kingdoms, both near and far, and everyone who heard their name feared them.
They gave kingship to whomever they wished and removed whomever they wished from power, and they became exceedingly great.
Yet despite all this, none of them undertook to wear a crown or put on purple robes to establish his rule.
Instead, they built a council house, and every day three hundred and twenty men entered the council to deliberate about the forces, so that they might keep the country prosperous.

Each year they appointed one trustworthy man from among them as ruler and head, to govern their entire land. Everyone obediently listened to this one man, and there was no strife or jealousy among them.

Then Judas selected men from each division: Eupolemus, of the family of Accos, the son of Jonathan, and Jason, the son of Eleazar. He sent them to the city of Rome to seek an alliance and support from them.
They were also to ask them to lift the yoke from their necks, for the Greeks had made the yoke of servitude heavy upon the necks of the Israelites.
They went to the territory of the Romans, and the journey was long. The envoys arrived and appeared before them in the council hall. They stood in their midst and began to deliver their message:

“Judas Maccabeus, his brothers, and the whole army of Judea speak with you about an alliance, to make you their supporters and to ask you for peace, so that you too may be willing to enroll us as your allies and friends.”
The proposal seemed good to them.
This is the copy of their decree, which they wrote for them on bronze tablets and sent to Jerusalem. They also kept a record for themselves of the alliance and peace:
“May peace and prosperity be with Judea and the Romans everywhere, at sea and on land. May sword and enemy be far from them.
If war first comes upon the Romans or any of their friends anywhere throughout their dominion,
the army of Judea shall quickly come to their aid, as circumstances indicate to them, with willing hearts.
They shall give nothing to the enemy or assist them with silver, gold, weapons, or ships. Thus it seemed good to the Romans that they should keep this command without taking bribes.
Likewise, if war comes upon the Jewish nation, the Romans shall quickly come to their aid with wholehearted resolve, as circumstances indicate to them.
They shall give the enemy no gold, silver, weapons, or ships, as it seemed good to the Romans. They shall keep these commands without deceit.
On these terms the Romans established their agreement with the army of the Jews.
If, after these terms, either party should consider removing or adding anything, they shall arrange whatever circumstances require by mutual consent, and their agreements shall remain binding.
Concerning the wrongs that King Demetrius inflicts upon them, we will write to him and say, ‘Why do you make the yoke heavy upon the necks of our allies and friends?
Know this: if they bring a complaint against you, we will render a just judgment and wage war against you, whether at sea or on land.’”

Demetrius heard nothing of how Nicanor and his army had fallen and been destroyed by them in battle. He again sent Bacchides and Alcimus, and with them the vanguard of his army, into the land of Judea.
They traveled along the road to Gilgal and came to fight at Mesaloth in the land of Arbela. They captured it and killed many people there.
In the first month of the one hundred and fifty-third year, they camped near Jerusalem.
They broke camp and reached Bereth with twenty thousand men armed with clubs and two thousand fully armed cavalry.
Judas was camped at Eleasa with three thousand picked, fully armed men.
When they saw the enormous host of the army, they were greatly afraid, and many deserted him. No one remained with Judas except eight hundred fully armed cavalry.

When Judas saw that his troops had deserted him and that battle was pressing upon him, he was distressed at heart, because there was no time to gather them again. He grew weak, lost heart, and collapsed.
He began to speak to those who remained, saying, “Come, let us attack them head-on. Perhaps we can inflict some damage on them.”

He kept advancing to attack, while the troops drew near and surrounded him. They began speaking to him about turning back and said, “Sir, you [?]; we cannot withstand them. For now, let us concentrate on saving our lives. Let us turn back and gather our brothers; then we will fight, even if we are few.”

Judas answered them and said, “Far be it from me to do such a thing—to flee from them! If our time has come, let us die bravely for our brothers, and let us not mingle the name of our cowardice with deeds of valor.”

The troops came out from their respective camps and drew up face-to-face against one another. Bacchides’ troops formed two fully armed divisions. The slingers and archers advanced ahead of the division, and the warriors had gone out in front.
But Bacchides was there on the right wing, hastening the troops forward urgently at the sound of the trumpet.
Judas’s company sounded the trumpet and came charging against them, until the earth shook from the tumult and shouting on both sides. The battle raged without interruption from morning until evening.
When Judas saw that Bacchides was there on the right wing with picked troops, he called forward the best-armed men from his own company, encouraged them, and immediately attacked.
At that moment he broke the right wing and drove it to the left. Then he drove them fleeing before him as far as the upper regions of Azotus.
When those on the left wing saw that the right wing had been broken before Judas’s men, they came and joined battle, surrounding Judas and his company.
There the wounded from both sides fell to the ground and lay writhing.
There Judas fell with the foremost warriors, and those who remained turned and fled.
The two brothers, Jonathan and Simon, returned, lifted Judas up, carried him away, and buried him in the tomb of their ancestors at Modein.
The children of Israel wept and lamented with great mourning. They grieved for many days and began to speak,
saying, “How has the mighty man, the deliverer of Israel, fallen and been destroyed!”
But the other battles, engagements, campaigns, and deeds of valor that Judas performed were not written in this book, for they were exceedingly numerous.
After Judas’s death, the lawless men [?] throughout the territory of the Israelites; those who practiced lawlessness sprang up, poured forth, and multiplied.
In those days there was a great famine, and the people went over to them of their own accord, and the land supported them.
Bacchides chose lawless men and appointed them as rulers over them.
They investigated, searched for Judas’s friends, and brought them to Bacchides. They took vengeance on them, tormented them, and subjected them to disgrace,
and they oppressed and mocked Israel, for such a thing had never happened since a prophet had appeared.
All Judas’s friends gathered and went to Jonathan Apphus and said,
“Your brother Judas has died, and there is no man like him to go out against the enemy and answer those who have come in hostility to oppress our nation.
But we have chosen you in his place, so that you may be ruler over us, lead us, and wage war against our enemies.”
Jonathan accepted the leadership at that time and rose up in place of his brother Judas.
When Bacchides learned of this, he sought to kill Jonathan and his brother Simon.
They fled into the wilderness of Tekoa and came and camped by the water at Asphar.
Bacchides learned of the Sabbath day, and he came and camped with his troops on the other side of the Jordan River.

He sent one of his brothers to them as commander of a large force, and they asked the Nabataeans, their friends, to take charge of their goods, their pack animals, and all the possessions that remained in their homeland.
The sons of Jambri, who were in Damascus, came out, seized John, and took him and his baggage away with them.

After these events, Jonathan and Simon, his brothers, were told that the sons of Jambri were celebrating a wedding and were bringing the bride from Abghaghatha, the daughter of one of the leading Canaanite nobles, with a great procession and an immense amount of finery.
They remembered John their brother, and went out and lay in ambush in a mountain ravine.
They looked up and saw a great procession and a large crowd approaching. The bridegroom came out with his groomsmen and his brothers, with trumpets, a drum, various musicians, and many armed men.
They came out of their ambush, killed many, and sent many away wounded. They put the armed men to flight, seized the goods and clothing as plunder, and looted the procession.
The wedding turned into mourning, and the sound of the musicians turned into grief and lamentation.
They exacted full revenge for their brother’s blood and returned to the meadow beside the Jordan River.
When Bacchides learned of this, he took his troops and marched against them, reaching the caves by the Jordan River.
Jonathan said to his troops, “Come, let us rise and fight for our lives, for today is not like yesterday or the day before.
Look, the troops are drawn up against us. There is neither a stronghold where we can hide nor open country where we can flee, and the Jordan River surrounds us.”

“Now come, let us raise our voices to heaven and charge against them. Perhaps you will escape from the hands of our enemies.” He said these words and immediately joined battle, charging against Bacchides.
Just as he was about to pour the souls into his own bosom [?], he fell backward.
And Jonathan and those with him rushed down from the ridge.
There Bacchides’ men struck down and killed a thousand men from Judas’ force, and returned to Jerusalem.

They began building fortified cities in the land of Judea, and the fortresses of Jericho, Emmaus, Beth-horon, Bethel, Minatharoth, and Stepha, strengthening them with walls, mighty gates, and sturdy bars.
They stationed garrisons there to act against the Israelites.
They fortified the city of Beth-zur, Gazara, and the citadel, and he stationed many troops there and stored abundant provisions.
He took the sons of the rulers of the land as hostages and placed them under guard in the citadel of Jerusalem.
In the hundred and tenth year, in the second month, Alcimus ordered the walls of the courts of the inner sanctuary to be demolished, and they began demolishing the work of the prophets.
At that time Alcimus was stricken, and his work was stopped. His jaws became dislocated, and he became speechless. He could not speak a word or give instructions concerning his household.
Alcimus died at that time in great torment.
When Bacchides saw that Alcimus had died, he returned to the king, and the land of Judea had rest for two years.
The lawless men plotted and said, “Look, Jonathan and those with him are living peacefully and without concern. Now come, let us bring Bacchides, and he will seize them all in a single night.”
They went and conferred with him.

He set out to come quickly with many troops. He secretly sent letters to his associates in Judea, telling them to seize Jonathan and those with him. But they could not do so, because he had been informed of their plans.
They seized fifty men from among the leaders of the evildoers in the land and slaughtered them on the spot.
Jonathan, Simon, and those with them fled to Bethbasi in the wilderness. They surrounded it with a trench and fortified it.
And when Bacchides saw this, his strength was failing, and he came to lay siege.
He attacked Bethbasi and fought for many days, and they made siege engines and set them up around it.
Jonathan left his brother Simon in that city and went out into the countryside, and came [?].
He struck down Odomera and his brothers and the sons of Phasiron in their tents, and began to go out and strike the troops.
Simon and those with him went out and set fire to the siege engines.
They fought a battle against Bacchides, and his forces were defeated by them, for that plan and his attack came to nothing.
He became furiously angry with the lawless men who had advised him to invade their land. He killed many of them and decided to return to his own land, from which he had come.
When Jonathan learned of this, he sent messengers after him and spoke with him about peacefully making a covenant and returning all the captives to him.
He agreed and did as Jonathan had proposed to him, and swore to him, “I will never again seek to harm you as long as I live.”
He returned the captives he had previously taken from the land of Judea, and went to his own country. He never again attempted to return to their territory.
The sword ceased from Israel. Jonathan settled in Michmash, and Jonathan began to judge his people and destroy the lawless people from Israel.
In the one hundred and sixtieth year, Alexander, son of Antiochus Epiphanes, came up and took the city of Ptolemais. They welcomed him, and he reigned there.
King Demetrius heard that he had gathered many troops and had gone out to engage him in battle.
Demetrius sent him peaceful words so that they would honor him.
“Let us hurry,” he said, “to make a peaceful covenant with him before Alexander has made a covenant with them concerning us.”
“I know that he will remember the wrongs we inflicted on him, his brothers, and his nation.”
He gave him authority to gather troops and prepare weapons, so that he would be his ally in battle, and ordered that the hostages in the citadel be handed over to him.
Jonathan came to Jerusalem and read the letter before all the people and before those who were there in the fortress.
They were greatly afraid because they heard that the king had given him authority to gather troops.
Nevertheless, they brought the hostages before him, and he gave them back to their families.
Jonathan settled in Jerusalem and began to rebuild and restore the city.
He said to those working on the construction of the walls, “Build,” he said, “the wall and Mount Zion on all four sides with blocks of hard stone.” And they did so.
The foreigners who were in the fortresses that Bacchides had built at that time fled.
He left them in their respective places and went to the land from which he came.
Some who had abandoned the law and the commandments remained in Beth-zur, because it was a stronghold.
When King Alexander heard of the good news that Demetrius had sent to Jonathan, they told him about the battles Jonathan had fought bravely with his brothers and the hardships they had endured.
And he said, “Can we find such a man anywhere? Come, let us make him our friend and supporter.”
And he ordered a letter to be written to them in these words:
“King Alexander to his brother Jonathan, greetings.
We have been informed about you that you are a man of courage and strength, and that you are worthy to be our friend.

We have therefore appointed you today as high priest of your nation, and you are to be called the king’s friend.” And he sent him a gold crown and purple garments. “Now remain in our covenant and keep faith with us in friendship. Farewell.”
And Jonathan took that splendid robe and put it on in the one hundred and sixty-seventh year, at the annual Feast of Tabernacles. They gathered troops, prepared weapons, and rejoiced.
And Demetrius heard these words and was greatly distressed.
And he said, “What have we done, that we did not make them our supporters? Now Alexander has acted quickly, spoken to them of peace, and made Judea a strong support for himself.”
“Now take this, and let us also write to them words of encouragement, honors, and gifts, so that they will come to our aid.”
And he sent them a letter in these words: “King Demetrius to the Jewish nation, greetings.
We have heard that you have kept the covenant and agreements you made with us, have remained steadfast in our friendship, and have not helped the enemy, and we rejoiced.
Now remain steadfast and keep that same faith with us.
And we will repay you with many exemptions and give you many gifts.
We will free you and exempt every Jew from taxes, the tax on salt [?], the crown taxes, and the payment of a third of the grain.

And whatever revenue came from half the yield of the vineyard and the trees, I remit to you from this day onward, including in the three districts added to you, and in Samaria and Galilee, from now on and forever.
And Jerusalem shall remain consecrated, holy, and exempt, together with its surrounding territory; the tithe and toll shall be remitted to you.
And authority over the inner fortress shall be given to the high priest, and he shall station in it men whom he himself chooses to guard it.

And every Jewish person from the land of Judea who is found in captivity anywhere in my kingdom shall be released freely, without ransom, and exempted from all taxes on produce, customs duties, and levies on pack animals.
And all the annual festivals, Sabbaths, new moons, the days before a festival, and the three days after each festival shall be tax-free for all Jews who are in my kingdom.
No one shall have authority to demand payment from or harass anyone over any claim of mine.
And they shall serve in the foremost ranks of the royal army, among six hundred thousand soldiers, and they shall receive payments as is customary for the foremost royal troops and the nobles.
