And those among them who are faithful shall be confirmed by royal authority. Their rulers and overseers shall be from among their own people. They shall live according to their own laws, as the king commanded for the land of Judea.

And the three districts previously assigned to the Judeans from the land of the Samaritans shall be returned to Judea, and the two shall be counted as one district, so that no other ruler shall have authority over them except the high priest.
And the city of Ptolemais shall be given to them as a gift dedicated to the sanctuary in Jerusalem, to meet the expenses incurred there in the sanctuary.
And I will give fifteen thousand weights of silver each year from the royal treasury, from whatever sources are appropriate.
All the provisions they were unable to supply shall come from the royal treasury, as with the former nations.”

From now on they shall give this from the royal funds. In addition, the five thousand weights of silver that they receive from the sanctuary’s income each year shall be remitted, for this belongs to the priests and attendants.

“Anyone who flees for refuge to the temple in Jerusalem, or who is anywhere within its boundaries, and owes anything to the royal treasury shall have it forgiven, and they themselves shall be set free.”
Whatever has been damaged or destroyed among the sacred buildings shall be rebuilt and restored, and the cost shall be paid from the royal treasury.
They shall rebuild the wall of Jerusalem and strengthen it all around, and the cost shall be paid from the royal treasury. All the walls of the fortresses of Judea shall also be rebuilt.

When Jonathan and the people heard these words, they neither trusted them nor accepted them, because they remembered the great evils he had committed in Jerusalem and the severe oppression with which his people had afflicted them.

Instead, they gladly agreed to the peace offered by Alexander, because he had been the first to approach them with words of peace. They were his comrades in arms and his supporters throughout their lives.
The king mustered his forces and gathered many troops to wage war against Demetrius.
The two kings came and clashed with one another. Demetrius’ army turned to flee, and Alexander prevailed over them.
He pressed the battle fiercely against them until sunset. There, on that day, Demetrius fell before Alexander. They struck and routed his forces and brought the matter to an end that day.
Alexander sent messengers to the land of the Egyptians, saying, “My dominion has returned to me.” He sent a message to King Ptolemy in these words: “Let this be known to you, king of the Egyptians:

My dominion has returned to me, and I have sat on the throne of my fathers. I have taken my authority into my own hands, struck and routed Demetrius with his troops, and brought my land back under my rule.
In battle I struck and routed him and his troops, and I have sat on the throne of his kingdom.
Now come, let us establish a firm peace between us. Give me your daughter in marriage, so that she may be worthy of me and I may be worthy to become your son-in-law.”
The king of the Egyptians replied, saying, “The day on which you returned to the land of your ancestors and sat on the royal throne of your fathers is a day of good fortune.

I am ready and willing to do all this as you have written to me. But come, let us meet face to face in the city of Ptolemais, so that we may see one another, and I will make you my son-in-law, as you have said.”
King Ptolemy left the land of the Egyptians with his daughter Cleopatra and came to the city of Ptolemais in the one hundred and sixty-second year.

The two kings met face to face, and he gave him his daughter Cleopatra. They celebrated the wedding in the city of Ptolemais with lavish preparations and great splendor, according to the custom of kings.
Alexander sent letters to Jonathan, asking him to come to him.
Jonathan set out and went with great splendor to the city of Ptolemais. He appeared before the two kings with magnificent gifts and found favor with them.
Lawless men from Jerusalem gathered against him to accuse him, but the king paid no attention to them.
The king ordered Jonathan to be stripped of his own clothes. They dressed him in purple, and the king seated him beside himself.

He said to the officials, “Now go with him and have a herald proclaim throughout all the cities that no one may dare to bring an accusation against him, and no one may trouble him even with a single word.”
When all his slanderers saw his splendor, heard the herald’s proclamation, and saw that he was dressed in purple, they fled, hid, and disappeared.
The king honored him among his foremost friends and appointed him commander of the army and governor.
Jonathan went to Jerusalem, full of joy and peace.
Then, in the one hundred and sixty-fifth year, Demetrius, the son of Demetrius, came from Crete to the land of his ancestors.
Alexander was deeply distressed and returned to the city of Antioch.

Demetrius appointed Apollonius there, who had previously been in charge of Lower Syria. He gathered many troops and came and encamped near Jamnia. He sent a message to Jonathan the high priest, saying:
“You alone stand exalted and proud over us, and because of you I have become an object of ridicule and scorn. Why do you lord it over us from those mountains of yours?
Now, please, if you trust in your troops, come down here to the plain to meet us, so that we may face one another, for I too have troops from the cities here with me.
Now inquire, put it to the test, and see who I am and who those who help you are. They say, ‘You have no footing in battle against us, for your ancestors were defeated twice in their own land.’
And now you cannot withstand so much cavalry on the plain, where there is no bush to hide in, no place to flee, no rock for shelter, and no pebble at hand to throw.”

When Jonathan heard this message from Apollonius, he became angry in his heart and immediately rose to his feet. He selected the very best of his troops, about ten thousand men, and went out from Jerusalem. His brother Simon came to meet him and lent him a hand in support.
They came to the city of Joppa. The citizens shut the gates against them, because guards appointed by Apollonius were stationed over them. They attacked and laid siege to the city.
Out of fear they opened the gates, and Jonathan’s men entered and took control of the city.
When Apollonius heard this, he equipped himself and made preparations, taking with him three thousand fully armed men and many other troops.
He went toward the region of Azotus, keeping close to the plain because he trusted in his troops. Jonathan followed him to engage him in battle.
He left a thousand horsemen in ambush behind him.

When Jonathan saw that they had laid an ambush behind him, his men came, blocked off and surrounded the stronghold of the ambushers, and set up a barrier around them. They stood guard from morning until evening, as Jonathan had commanded them.
The horsemen grew weary and exhausted and dispersed.
Simon took a secret route with his division, advanced along the ravine, and fell upon them. While they were resting and exhausted, he attacked them and killed many of them there in the ambush.

He drove many cavalrymen fleeing before them across the plain, pursuing them as far as the region of Azotus. He pressed them with such urgency and distress that the fugitives went into the temple of Dagon and took refuge there.
Jonathan arrived with his troops and surrounded the temple of Dagon and the city of Azotus. He plundered the cities around it and burned the temple of Dagon with those who had taken refuge in it.
Those who fell by the sword, together with those who were burned, numbered about eight hundred thousand men.
Jonathan broke camp, moved on from there, and came and encamped in the region of Ashkelon. They came out of the city to meet him with honors.
Jonathan returned to Jerusalem with his force and much plunder, for he brought a great amount of booty and spoil from his enemies.
When Alexander heard this, he honored Jonathan still more.
He had a gold buckle brought to him, of the kind that the king’s brothers customarily wore, and gave him Ekron with all its territory as a hereditary possession.
The king of Egypt mustered and gathered troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore, and many ships. He sought to seize Alexander’s kingdom by deceit and add it to his own kingdom.
He entered the regions of Syria with peaceful words, and they opened their gates to him and went out to meet him, for King Alexander had given orders to do so, since he was Alexander’s father-in-law.
Whenever Ptolemy entered the cities, he left a garrison from his own troops in each city.

When they approached the city of Azotus, they showed him the temple of Dagon burned down, the city and its surrounding settlements burned during the war, and the burned corpses that had been brought together and piled in heaps along the road.
They told the king everything Jonathan had done and spoke against him, but the king remained silent.
Jonathan came to meet the king in the city of Joppa with great pomp. They greeted one another and spent that day together.
Jonathan accompanied the king as far as the region of the river called Eleutherus. Then Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.
King Ptolemy took possession of the coastal cities as far as Seleucia, and he devised an evil plan against Alexander.

He sent letters to King Demetrius, saying, “Come, let us make a covenant with one another and establish an alliance. I will give you my daughter, whom King Alexander has as his wife, and you will rule over your father’s kingdom.
For I regret having given him my daughter in marriage, because he plotted to kill me.”
He spoke against him in this way because he himself had set his sights on Alexander’s kingdom.

He took his daughter away and gave her to Demetrius. He broke with Alexander and made his hostility known. Ptolemy entered and took possession of the coastal cities and Seleucia, and he plotted evil against Alexander.
He entered the city of Antioch and put on the crown of Asia. He was crowned with two crowns, the crown of Asia and the crown of Egypt.
But King Alexander was in the region of Cilicia at that time, because its people were rebelling against him.
When Alexander heard this, he advanced against him to wage war. Ptolemy went out to meet him with a large army and defeated him.
Alexander fled to the region of Arabia to hide there and escape from him, and King Ptolemy rose to power.
Zabdiel the Arab came, cut off Alexander’s head, and had it taken to King Ptolemy.
Ptolemy died on the third day, and those stationed in the strongholds were killed by the inhabitants of the strongholds.
Demetrius became king in the one hundred and sixty-seventh year.
In those days Jonathan gathered troops in Judea to attack the citadel in Jerusalem, and they set up many siege engines around it.
Then some lawless men who were enemies of the Jewish nation went to tell the king that Jonathan had set up siege engines around the citadel, surrounded it, and prepared to take it.

When he heard this, he became very angry, set out, and came to Ptolemais. He sent letters to Jonathan, ordering him not to keep the citadel under siege any longer, but to set out himself and come quickly to him in the city of Ptolemais, so that they could meet there.
When Jonathan heard this, he ordered the watch around the citadel to be strengthened still further. He himself took chosen, wise men from the elders of the people and from the priests.
He equipped himself with gifts of gold and silver, risked his life, and went to meet the king in the city of Ptolemais. He found favor with him,
although many of the lawless men brought accusations against him.
The king honored him as his predecessors had done and greatly exalted him before all his friends.
He confirmed him in the office of high priest and in all the other honors he had previously held. He appointed him among his chief friends.
Jonathan asked the king to exempt Judea, the three districts, and Samaria from tribute, and undertook to give him three hundred talents.
The king was pleased, and concerning all these matters he ordered letters to be given to Jonathan in the following form:
“King Demetrius to his brother Jonathan: Greetings.”
We wrote a copy of this decree to our brother Lasthenes, and we have written to you in the same terms so that you may know.
King Demetrius to Lasthenes, his father: Greetings.
We have judged it right to grant relief and favors to the Jewish nation, our allies, comrades in arms, and faithful friends, in return for the upright loyalty they have maintained toward us.

We have established the boundaries of Judea, and the three districts of Ephraim, Lydda, and Ramathaim have been added to Judea from the territory of Samaria. All revenues lawfully due from them shall belong to those serving in Jerusalem, in place of the royal revenues that came from them year by year from the crops of the land and the fruit of the trees.
And whatever other royal assessments, tithes, customs duties, or revenues are due to the royal treasury, whether the tax on [?] or the crown tax,
we shall remit all these for them, and none of these concessions shall ever be disregarded.
Now take care to make a copy of this decree and give it to Jonathan, so that he may place it in the sacred treasury, in a suitable and conspicuous place.

When King Demetrius saw that the whole land had submitted to him and that there was no one in the country who opposed his commands, he ordered the troops to be discharged to their own homes, except for the troops from distant nations and the [?] contingent from the islands [?]. Then all the troops of the nations became hostile to him.

There was a man named Tryphon who belonged to Alexander’s party. When he saw that all the troops were grumbling against Demetrius, he went to Imalkue the Arab, who was bringing up Alexander’s young son Antiochus.

He hurried to him so that he would give him the child, whom he would bring back and make king in his father's place. He told him everything Demetrius had done and all the hostility the troops had shown. He stayed there with him for many days.
Jonathan sent word to King Demetrius, asking him to order the removal of the troops stationed in the citadel and in the fortresses, because they were hostile to Israel.
Demetrius sent word to Jonathan, saying, “I shall do not only this for you and your nation, but I shall also bestow great honor on your nation, if only I find the opportunity.
Now you would do well to send me a contingent to support me, because my troops have deserted me.”
When Jonathan heard this, he immediately sent a contingent of three thousand chosen, fully armed men to support the king in the city of Antioch. The king was glad when they arrived to serve him.

When the citizens heard this, they gathered from their various quarters in the center of the city, about one hundred and twenty thousand of them. They rushed against the king, intending to kill him on the spot.
He fled from them, and they quickly seized all the narrow passages through the city, drew up for battle, and began fighting.
The Israelite contingent was informed. They gathered around the king’s palace, called out to one another, and spread throughout the city.

They struck down, killed, and slaughtered about ten thousand men. They set fire to all the wooden buildings of his palace, took their goods and possessions as plunder, brought the king into their midst, and rescued him from their hands.

When the remaining force in the city saw that the Israelite contingent had gained the upper hand over them and defeated them at will, they lost heart, grew faint, and faltered in their plans. They began crying out to the king in pleading voices, saying,
“Give us your hand in peace, and let this raging contingent stop slaughtering the people of our city.”

They said these words and each threw down his weapons at the feet of the fighting men. The Israelite force rose in glory before the king and all his troops, and they returned to Jerusalem with great renown and much plunder.
King Demetrius sat on the throne of his kingdom, and the whole land trembled before him.
But he proved false to the Israelites in everything he had promised them. He completely estranged himself from Jonathan and did not repay him for his loyal service.
After this, Tryphon returned, and with him was the young Antiochus, who became king and sat on the royal throne.
All the troops that Demetrius had dispersed gathered to him. They fought a battle against Demetrius and put him to flight in defeat.
Tryphon came, took the elephants, and captured the city of Antioch.

The young Antiochus ordered a letter to be drawn up for Jonathan, saying, “I have appointed you to the office of high priest and confirmed your authority over the four laws, and we have numbered you among our closest and foremost friends.”
He had golden cups and vessels for the temple sent to him. He also gave him permission to drink from golden cups, to wear purple, and to wear splendid insignia like the insignia of kings.
He ordered that his brother Simon be appointed governor and military commander over the region from Tyre to the borders of Egypt.

Jonathan went out to travel beyond the Jordan River and through the cities, and all the Syrian forces gathered around him to support him. He came to the region of Ashkelon, and the citizens came out to meet him with great praise.

From there he went to Gaza, but the people of Gaza shut their gates against him. He encamped around them and set fire to their villages, and his men carried off their goods and possessions as plunder.

Then the people of Gaza came and stood before him, pledged their allegiance to him, and handed over the sons of their leaders as hostages. He took them and had them brought to Jerusalem, while he himself passed through the land toward Damascus.
Jonathan heard that Demetrius's commanders had arrived at Kedesh in the territory of Galilee with large forces, intending to remove him from his position.
He left his brother Simon in charge of the land and went out himself to meet them.
Simon attacked Beth-zur, besieged it for many days, and kept its people confined.
They began to beg him to make a treaty with them. He pledged his word to them, brought them out of there, and stationed guards in the city.
Jonathan came with his forces and encamped beside the waters of Gennesaret. Early in the morning he went to the plain of Hazor.
A force of foreigners met him there on the plain. They laid an ambush for him: half went into hiding, and half confronted him.
The men lying in ambush rose from their positions and came after them, surrounding Jonathan and his forces.
They put Jonathan’s forces to flight, and no one remained with him except Mattathias son of Absalom and Judas son of Scaph, the commanders of the forces.
Jonathan grasped the collar of his robe and tore it, and put earth on his head.
He attacked them with great fury and defeated them.
Then all those who had fled returned to the same place and drove the enemy before them as far as their camp at Kadesh. They reached the camp of the foreigners and fell upon it.
That day they struck down and killed about three thousand armed horsemen. Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.
When Jonathan saw that circumstances favored him, he called chosen men and sent them to the city of the Romans to renew the treaty of peace with them.
He also wrote letters of the same kind to the Spartans and to various other places.

The envoys went and reached the city of the Romans. They appeared before them in the council chamber and said, “Jonathan the high priest and the Jewish nation have sent us to you to renew the former peace, so that we may be allies and support one another as before.”
They agreed and approved, and gave them letters for the various places, so that they might be escorted safely to the land of Judea.
This is a copy of the letters Jonathan wrote to the ruling princes and their governors:
“Jonathan the high priest, the council of elders together with the people, the priests, and the assembled forces and army of the Jewish nation, to the Spartans our brothers: greetings.
“Letters were previously sent to Onias the high priest from King Darius, your king, stating that you are our allies, brothers, and friends, as the copies show us.
Onias received the man who had been sent with great honor and took a letter in which he described us as his comrades in arms, supporters, and beloved friends.
Now we, being fully supplied and lacking nothing, were encouraged by these letters of yours.
To send and renew once more that same agreement of kinship, so that we may not become estranged from you, for much time has passed since the old agreements that you made with us.

Now we always remember you without fail at the annual festivals and on other fitting days, during the sacrifices that we offer. We remember you in our prayers, as it is right and proper to remember our brothers.
And we rejoice in your glory.
Now, many hardships of war have surrounded us, and the kings around us have made war against us.
Yet until now we have not wished to trouble you in this warfare—neither you nor those around you who are our friends and allies in arms.
For we had help from heaven, and we escaped from the hands of our enemies, and our enemies were defeated before us.
Now we chose Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason and sent them to the Romans to renew the former treaty of agreement, mutual support, friendship, and brotherhood.
We instructed them to visit you, greet you, and present this letter concerning the renewal of our brotherly love.
Now you will do well to give orders that a reply be made to us.
And this is a copy of the letter that they sent back to Onias the priest.
The king of the Spartans, to Onias the high priest: Greetings.
Ancient books have been found concerning the Spartans and the Jews, stating that they are brothers, equal to one another, and descended from Abraham.
Now that we have learned this, you will do well to write to us continually about your peace and well-being.
And we will write to you about ours. Our goods, possessions, and all our livestock are yours, just as yours are ours. Now we give this instruction: continually maintain this relationship with us.
And Jonathan heard that Demetrius's commanders had returned with larger forces than before to come against him in battle.
He set out from Jerusalem and marched against them. He met them and attacked them in the region of Hamath, for he did not allow them to reach his own land and disturb it.
He sent scouts into their camp, and they reported to him: “They are preparing to fall upon us during the night.”

When the sun had set, Jonathan ordered the troops to remain armed, awake, ready, and assembled together until morning for battle. They posted sentries around themselves, secured their position, and stood ready for battle.

When the enemies heard that they had prepared for battle during the night, they became afraid and terrified, and their hearts failed them. They lit closely spaced fires everywhere, and they themselves fled during the night.
Jonathan and his troops did not know that they had fled, because he saw the blazing fires and thought that they were still in their places.
Afterward, although he pursued them, he could not overtake them, because they had crossed the river Eleutherus.
Then Jonathan turned away from them against the Arabs called the Zabadeans. He struck them, killed them, routed their forces, and took their goods and possessions as plunder.
And he turned toward the region of Damascus.
And he reached Ashkelon and took all the strongholds around it. Then he turned toward the region of Joppa and hurried to bring the troops inside.
For he heard that the fortresses were giving their support to Demetrius, and he stationed guards and officers over them.
Jonathan returned, selected troops, and summoned the council of elders for consultation, wishing to build the fortifications of Judea.

and to build up high between the citadel and the city. He wanted to put a great, high barrier between them and the city, so that they would be isolated and would neither give nor receive, neither buy nor sell.
And they gathered to rebuild the city and the parts of the walls that had fallen by the [?] torrents, on the wooded side, which is called Chaphenatha.
And Simon began to build Adida in the Shephelah. He fortified it, fitted it with gates, and secured it with bars.
And Tryphon sought to become king over the regions of Asia, to put on a crown, and to lay hands on King Antiochus.
But he was afraid and apprehensive that Jonathan might not agree and might march against him in battle. He sought a way to seize him and destroy him.
He set out and came to the region of Bethsan. Jonathan went out to meet him with forty thousand chosen men, armed and ready for battle, and arrived at Bethsan.
And Tryphon saw that Jonathan had arrived with many troops, and he was afraid to lay hands on him.
Then he received him with honor, presented him to all his friends, gave him gifts, and ordered his troops to obey him.
He began to speak with Jonathan and said, “Why have you slaughtered so many troops, when there was no fighting going on?

Now send your troops away, each to his own place, and choose a few men to stay with you and accompany you at all times. Come with me to Ptolemais, and I will hand it over to you, along with the other fortresses and their troops, so that they will be under your control. Then I will return, for this is precisely why I came.”
And Jonathan trusted him and did as he ordered. He sent the troops away, each to his own place in the land of Judea.
He kept about three thousand men with him. Then he left two thousand of them in the land of Galilee, and he himself went with Tryphon with one thousand.
When Jonathan entered Ptolemais, the citizens seized the gates and shut him inside, and they put to the sword everyone who had entered with him.
And Tryphon sent troops against Jonathan’s troops who were in the land of Galilee and on the great plain, to go and destroy all Jonathan’s forces.
When they learned that he had been shut inside and that everyone with him had perished, they took courage and advanced into battle together as one body.
When the soldiers who had advanced against them saw that they were fighting wholeheartedly for their own lives, they became afraid, left them alone, and turned back.
And they reached the land of Judea in peace. They lamented and wept for Jonathan and the troops who had been with him, and they were in great fear. All Israel sat in mourning and wept for Jonathan.
All the nations around them began seeking to destroy them, for they said:
“They have no leader or ruler over them to wage war against us. Now come, let us attack them and erase their memory from the earth.”
And Simon heard that Tryphon had gathered many troops to come against the land of Judea and destroy them.
He found that there was great dread and fear. He himself went up to Jerusalem and also gathered the people.

He encouraged them and said, “You yourselves know how much work I, my brothers, and my father’s household have done, how many battles we have fought, and how much hardship we have endured for the sacred things of the law and the city.
For the sake of Israel and all of you, all my brothers have perished, and I alone remain.
And now, far be it from me to [?] and feel sorry for myself at any time of distress. I am no better in courage than my brothers.

Nevertheless, I will take courage to seek vengeance for the nation, for the holy things of the law, and for our wives and children. For look, all the nations have gathered to come and wipe out our memory from the earth.
As he said this, he encouraged and comforted the hearts of all the people.
They answered, speaking in a loud voice, and said, “You are our leader in place of Judas and your brother Jonathan.
Fight our battles, and we will obey you in everything you say.”
He gathered all the fighting men and hurried to build the wall of Jerusalem.
He sent Jonathan son of Absalom with a large force to the city of Joppa. Jonathan drove the guards out of it, entered it himself, fortified it, and guarded it.
After this, Tryphon set out from the city of Ptolemais with a large force to come into the land of Judea, bringing Jonathan with him under close guard.
Simon was encamped at Adida, facing the plain.
Tryphon learned that Simon had risen to take the place of his brother Jonathan and was ready for battle. He appointed messengers and sent them to him, saying:
“Jonathan is being detained here because of the money he owed the royal treasury.
Now have a hundred talents of silver brought here, and have two of his sons brought to me, so that when we release him he will not rebel against us.”
Simon knew that he was speaking deceitfully to him, but he had the silver and the boys sent, lest hostility arise between the people and himself.
“And they will say that he was greedy for the money and did not send the young men, and the man perished.”
Then he had the young men and the hundred talents sent. Nevertheless, Tryphon proved false and did not release Jonathan.
After this, Tryphon came into the regions of the land to move around and destroy them. They went around by the road to Adora. Simon, with his army, blocked his advance wherever he went against him.
Those in the citadel in Jerusalem sent messengers to Tryphon, urging him to come to them through the wilderness and supply the fortress with provisions.
Tryphon prepared to come in with his troops that night, but there was a heavy snowfall, and because of it he could not enter. He broke camp and came into the region of Gilead.
When he approached Baskama, he killed Jonathan there, and Jonathan was buried there.
Tryphon returned from there and came into his own country.
Simon sent to retrieve the bones of his brother Jonathan from there. They brought him back and buried him at Modein, in the city of their ancestors.
All Israel lamented and wept for him, and they mourned for many days.
There he built a structure over the tomb of his father and his brothers, raising it high with dressed stonework all around.
He erected pyramids upon it, facing one another, and placed three [?] there for his father and his brothers, facing one another.

With tall pillars and enclosing latticework, he made an everlasting name for himself. On the sides of the latticework he placed carvings in the likeness of ships, so that they would be visible to those passing across the sea in ships,
beside the tombs that they built at Modein, to this day.
Tryphon dealt treacherously with the young King Antiochus and killed him.
And he reigned with him, took the crown of the people of Asia, and carried out great [?] in the land.
Simon rebuilt the fortresses of Judea, raised their walls, erected towers, secured them with gates and bars, and strengthened the fortresses with stores of provisions.
Simon summoned chosen men and sent them to Demetrius so that he would grant the land an exemption, for everything Tryphon did was plunder.
King Demetrius sent him a reply in accordance with these words and wrote a royal letter in the following form:
King Demetrius to Simon the high priest, friend of kings, and to the entire council of elders of the Jewish nation: Greetings.

“We have received the gold crown and the gift that you had brought to us. We are ready to establish a lasting peace and to write to the officials responsible for collecting taxes, so that they may cancel your debts.
Whatever we have confirmed for you shall remain in force, and the fortresses you are building shall belong to you.
We forgive you the offenses you have committed, willingly or unwillingly, up to this day. The crown tribute you owe and any other tax collected from Jerusalem shall no longer be collected.”
If any of you are suitable and worthy to be entered on our register, let them be entered freely. And let there be peace between us and you.
In the one hundred and seventieth year, the yoke of the Gentiles was lifted from the people of Israel.
The people began to write in their records and their contracts of sale: “In the first year, in the days of Simon, the great high priest, leader, and commander of the Jewish nation.”
In those days he surrounded the city of the people of Gaza and besieged it with troops. He constructed siege engines there, brought them up to the wall, and demolished a tower.
They came out of the siege engine and rushed into the city, and there was a great uproar in the city.
All the citizens, together with their wives and children, rushed forward, crying out, tearing their collars, and raising their voices to call upon Simon.
They begged him to lend them a hand, so that they would not be judged according to their wickedness, but that he would have compassion on them according to his mercy.

Simon relented, stopped the fighting, and ordered them to be driven out of the city. They cleansed the palaces of all the filth and defilement of their idols, and then he entered with rejoicing and praise.
He removed every defilement from it and settled there men who would keep the law. He also fortified it and built many kinds of palace buildings there.

Those in the citadel in Jerusalem were confined, hard-pressed, and besieged. They could neither go out nor come in, neither buy nor sell. In their distress they were starving to death, and many of them perished.
They cried out to Simon, begging to stand before him. He lent them a hand, brought them out of there, and cleansed the citadel of all their defilements.

He entered it on the twentieth day of the second month, in the one hundred and seventieth year. He entered with praise and thanksgiving, with palm branches, amid the joyful sound of trumpets and flutes, because a great enemy had been crushed and removed from the house of Israel.
He ordered that this festival be celebrated every year on that day with joy and rejoicing.
He fortified the temple hill alongside the citadel, and he himself lived there with his own troops.
Simon saw that his son Jonathan was a mature man who had come of age. He appointed him ruler, commander, and leader over all the troops, and stationed him in the region of Gazara.

In the one hundred and seventy-second year, King Demetrius gathered troops and crossed into the regions of the Medes and Parthians to seek support there, so that he could return and wage war against Trypho.
When Arsaces, king of the Persians and Parthians, heard that Demetrius had entered the borders of his country, he sent one of his commanders to go and arrest him.
He went and struck down and destroyed Demetrius’s forces and captured him. He came, brought Demetrius, and held him before Arsaces, who ordered him to be bound in royal fetters and put in prison.
The land rested in peace throughout all the days of Simon. He added blessing upon blessing to their nation and ruled over the provinces.
He gathered many captives and ruled over the regions of Gazara and Beth-zur and over the strongholds.
They cultivated their land in peace, and the land yielded its fruit, and every planted tree yielded its produce abundantly.
The elders sat in the public squares, giving speeches about good things and discussing them with one another. The young men were clothed in glory, adorned with equipment for war.
They strengthened the cities with provisions and equipped themselves with protective armor and weapons, until the fame of his glory reached the ends of the earth.
He made peace, and Israel rejoiced with great joy.
Each sat under their own vine and under their own fig tree, and no one frightened them.
All who fought against them disappeared from the land, and the kings were crushed in their days.
He established and strengthened the lowly among the people. He sought vindication for the law and wiped out all the wicked and lawless from the land.
He glorified the sanctuary and increased the equipment for its service.
News reached the city of the Romans and the territory of the Spartans that Jonathan had died, and they were deeply grieved.
But when they heard that Simon, his brother, stood at the head of the priesthood in his place and firmly held dominion over the provinces and the cities within them,
they appointed messengers and wrote letters on bronze tablets to renew the old friendship that they had pledged and established with Judas and with Jonathan, his brother.
When they brought them, they read them before the people of Jerusalem. This is a copy of the letters that the Spartans sent:

The rulers and leaders of the Spartans, together with the great city, to Simon the high priest, to the council of elders of the Israelites, to the priests, and to the whole community of the Jews, our brothers: greetings.
The messengers sent from you to us told us of your glory and honor, and we rejoiced at their arrival.

We recorded your messages in the books of the deliberations of our assembly as follows: Numenius, son of Antiochus, and Antipater, son of Jason, messengers of the Jews, came to us to renew friendship with our nation.

It seemed good to all the Spartans to receive the men with great honor and to place a copy of their words in a prominent place in the books of the deliberations of the Spartan assembly. They also made a reply to the letters addressed to Simon the high priest.
Again, after these events, Simon sent messengers back to Rome with a great gift and a golden shield weighing a thousand talents, so that they might go and confirm the former friendship and alliance.
When the assembly of the Romans heard this, they began to deliberate and say, “Now, what favors shall we return to Simon and his sons for their favors?

For he, his brothers, and his father’s household confirmed their friendship with us. He struck down his enemies and firmly established us as his friends and allies.” They confirmed his freedom and wrote this on bronze tablets, and they erected a monument for him on Mount Zion.
This is a copy of the document they wrote in the one hundred and seventieth year, on the eighteenth day of the month, in the third year of Simon's high priesthood, at Samareq.
In the presence of a great gathering of priests, the people, rulers of nations, and the council of elders of many provinces, it was made known to us that many battles had been fought in that land.

But Simon, son of Mattathias the high priest, of the descendants of Joarib, together with his brothers, put his life in the balance and gave himself to the struggle of battle. He stood against the enemies of their nation so that their holy places and their law would not be defiled, and he brought great glory to their nation.
Jonathan gathered their nation together and became their high priest. He died and was gathered to his ancestors.
Their enemies wished to invade their land and lay their hands on their holy things.

At that time Simon arose and fought on behalf of their nation. He spent great sums from his own treasury, supplied weapons and equipment for the fighting men of his nation, and stored up supplies and provisions for the army.

He fortified the cities of Judea, including Beth-zur, which was on the border of Judea. There he prepared and stored all the weapons and equipment needed to confront their enemies’ forces, and he stationed men of Judea there as guards.

He also fortified the city of Joppa, which was by the sea, and Gazara, which was on the border of Ashdod and had previously been held by their enemies. He settled men of Judea there and securely provided them with everything they needed.

When the people saw all these deeds of Simon and the glory he intended for the nation, they appointed him ruler and high priest because he had done all these things for them, and because of the righteousness and faithfulness he maintained toward his nation. In every circumstance he sought to raise up his people.

In his days he succeeded in wiping out the Gentiles from his land. Those who were in the citadel in Jerusalem would come out and go in, greatly defiling the area around the sanctuary, and great harm was done to the sanctuary. He confined them there and wiped them out.
He stationed and established guards there to protect the land and the city, and he raised it up.
Moreover, King Demetrius also confirmed his high priesthood.
Because of all this, he honored him greatly among his close friends.
For he had heard that the Jews were called friends, brothers, supporters, and allies in arms of the Romans, and that they had received Simon’s messengers with honor.
For the Jews themselves and the priests were pleased to agree to appoint him ruler and high priest forever, until a trustworthy prophet should arise.

He was to be their commander and leader, to care for the holy places, and to make appointments by his authority to oversee their affairs, their districts, their weapons and equipment, and their fortresses.

He was to care for the holy places, and all the nations were to obey them. All documents of the land were to be sealed in his name. He was to have the authority to wear purple and adorn himself with gold.
No one from the people or the priests was to have the authority to oppose his commands, to convene assemblies in his land without him, to wear purple, or to put on a gold brooch.
If anyone transgressed or disregarded any of these provisions, he was to be liable to death.
The people approved of acting toward Simon according to these provisions.
Simon accepted and agreed to stand at the head of the high priesthood, to be commander-in-chief and leader of the army of Judea, to be head of the priests, and to lead them all.
They ordered that this document be written on bronze tablets and placed in the stronghold, in a prominent and visible place within the sanctuary.
Copies of them were to be placed in the treasury, so that Simon and his sons would always have them in their possession.
Antiochus, son of King Demetrius, sent letters from the islands to Simon, the high priest and governor of the Jewish nation, and to his entire nation.
The letters were worded as follows: King Antiochus to Simon the great high priest and governor of the Jewish nation: Greetings.

For certain lawless men came and seized the kingdom of my ancestors. Now I am seeking to rebuild, restore, and establish that same kingdom as it was before. I am therefore gathering a large army and have prepared warships.
To go out and seek vengeance for my ancestors against the nations that harmed our land and destroyed our great cities.
Now I confirm for you every agreement concerning tribute that the former kings remitted to you, and any other payment due by the law of tribute shall be remitted to you.
We have also given orders that you shall have authority to mint your own coins in your land.
Jerusalem and your sanctuary shall be exempt from everything, and the weapons and equipment you have made and the fortresses you have fortified shall be yours.
All royal debts, revenues, and duties that used to come from there shall be yours from now on forever.
But when we attain our kingdom, we shall honor you, your nation, and your temple with great glory, so that your glory may be known throughout the whole earth.
In the one hundred and seventy-fourth year, Antiochus arrived in the land of his ancestors. All the troops gathered to him, and only a few remained with Tryphon.
Antiochus pursued him and drove him into Dor, on the seacoast.
All the troops abandoned him when they saw the troubles that had overtaken him.
Antiochus came and encamped around Dor with twelve thousand fighting men and eight thousand armed cavalry.
He blocked the seaward side with ships and pressed the city hard from both sea and land, and they allowed no one to leave.
Numenius and those with him came, bringing letters from the city of Rome to the kings of the land, in which the following was written:
Lucius, consul of the Romans, to King Ptolemy: greetings.
The elders from Judea came to us to renew the former bond of friendship as our allies and supporters. They were sent to us by Simon the high priest and the community of the Jews.
They brought us a gold shield weighing five thousand talents.

For this reason we thought it good to write to the kings of your land and to all your nations, so that no one should plan any harm against them or wage war against their cities and their land, and so that they should not join their enemies in battle.
We thought it good to accept the shield from them.
Now, if there are any lawless men who have fled from their land, hand them over to Simon the high priest, so that he may exact punishment according to their laws.
He also wrote in this way to King Demetrius, to Attalus, to Ariarathes, and to Arsaces.

To all the regions, as seemed good: to the Spartans, and to Delos, Myndos [?], Sicyon, Caria [?], Samos, Pamphylia, Lycia, Halicarnassus, Rhodes, Phaselis, Side, Arados [?], Gortyna [?], Cnidus, Cyprus, and Cyrene.
They also sent Simon the high priest a copy of the letters.

King Antiochus came and besieged Dor. Early in the morning he brought siege engines against it and attacked it. He kept Tryphon shut up inside under siege, and no one could go out from within or enter from outside.
Simon sent two thousand chosen, armed fighting men to support him, together with lavish gifts of gold and silver.
But he disregarded everything he had promised him and became estranged from him.
He sent Athenobius, one of his friends, to confer with him and say, “You have seized and firmly hold cities of my kingdom: the cities of Joppa and Gazara, and the citadel of Jerusalem.
You have devastated their territories and inflicted great harm upon their land. You have taken possession of many districts and cut off many provinces from my dominion.”
Now give up the cities, districts, regions, and their taxes, and everything you have forcibly taken from us outside the borders of Judea.

Otherwise, give five hundred talents of silver in exchange for them, and another five thousand talents for the taxes of the cities that you have withheld until today. Otherwise, we will come, attack you, drive you out, and devastate the land.

When Athenobius, the king’s friend, came to Jerusalem, he saw Simon’s splendor, his gold and silver vessels, and the equipment prepared for his many soldiers. He stood before him and delivered the king’s message with pomp.

Simon answered him, saying, “We have not entered anyone’s foreign land or unjustly entered anyone else’s territory. A violent hand invaded the allotted inheritance of our fathers, who were unjustly driven into exile by invincible enemies.
When we found an opportunity, we courageously sought it back.

But as for the city of Joppa and Gazara, which you demand, they did great harm within our country, and we sought vengeance. For this we will pay a penalty of one hundred talents.” And he gave him no answer to these words.
He returned to the king in anger and told him of Simon’s splendor and all the furnishings and equipment he had seen. This greatly angered the king.
Trypho fled to Orthosia.
The king appointed Cendebeus commander of the coastal region and assigned him many cavalry and infantry troops.
He commanded him to take up his position opposite Judea and to build strongholds in preparation for battle against the forces of the Israelites. The king himself was pursuing Tryphon.
Cendebeus set out and reached the region of Jamnia. He began stirring up the troops and sending them into Judea to take captives and kill. He also built Kedron.
He stationed many cavalry troops there so that they could invade Judea and block its roads, as the king had commanded.
John went up from Gazara and came to tell his father Simon what Cendebeus was doing.

Simon called his two sons, Judas and John, and said to them, “My brothers, my father’s household, and I have fought against Israel’s enemies from our youth until this very day. Everything we undertook succeeded in our hands, saving many of the people of Israel.
But now I have grown old, and you are capable of taking my place and my brother’s in my old age. Now go out and fight for our people, and may the power of help from heaven be with you.”
He selected about twenty thousand fully armed horsemen from the country and marched against Cendebeus.

They came and lodged that day in Modein. Early in the morning they entered the plain. There they saw many cavalry and infantry troops coming against him, and there was a ravine between the two armies.

He and his troops drew up in battle formation facing them. When he looked and saw that his troops were hesitating to cross the ravine, he himself advanced first. Then the troops sounded their trumpets together behind him.
He divided the cavalry into two companies among the infantry, and the cavalry was exceedingly numerous.
They sounded the trumpet, raised a shout, and attacked. Cendebeus was defeated, and many of his men fell wounded that day. Those who remained fled to the strongholds.
That day Judas was wounded, but John pursued the fugitives until he drove them into the region of Kedron, which Cendebeus had built.
They withdrew into the towers in the region of Azotus. He set them on fire, and about two thousand men were burned in that stronghold. He himself returned to the regions of Judea in peace.
Ptolemy son of Abubus had been appointed over the regions of the plain at Jericho, and he possessed a great deal of silver and gold.
For he was the high priest’s son-in-law.
He became proud in his heart and arrogant in his thoughts. He wanted to rule over the regions of the district and treacherously plotted against Simon and his sons to wipe them out.

Simon traveled through the districts, caring for them and seeing to their needs. He came down to Jericho, he himself and Mattathias and Judas and his sons, in the one hundred and seventy-seventh year, in the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat.
Ptolemy received them with deceitful honors in the town of Dok, which he had built, and held a feast for his guests. There he stationed men in ambush.

When Simon and his sons had eaten and drunk and become drunk, Ptolemy rose with the men he had hidden. They took their weapons, rushed upon Simon, and killed him there in the banquet hall, along with his sons and the servants who were with him.
They committed a great act of lawlessness and repaid good with evil.
Ptolemy wrote to the king to send troops to support him, so that he could hand over their towns and the tribute to them.
He sent half of them to the region of Gezer to remove John from there. He also wrote to the commanders, telling them to come and receive gold, silver, and many gifts from him.
He sent others to Jerusalem to hurry there and seize the Temple Mount.
One man made his way ahead to Gazara and brought John the news: “Your father and your brothers have perished, and he has also sent men against you deceitfully to kill you.”
When he heard this, he was greatly astonished and bewildered. He seized those men and killed them there, because he learned that they had come deceitfully to destroy him.
As for any other accounts concerning John—his battles and wars, his other brave deeds, his building of walls, or his good works—
all these are written in the records of the priests, from the time he became high priest after his father. The First Book of Maccabees is finished.
